articles.title: How a series of miscalculations restarted Saudi Arabia’s war in Yemen - CNN
articles.summary: How a series of miscalculations restarted Saudi Arabia’s war in Yemen  CNNIran war updates: Saudi-led coalition hits Houthis; Putin, Trump talk Iran  Al JazeeraDays of Deadly Houthi Attacks Show Saudi Arabia’s Vulnerabilities  The New York TimesAnalysis • A Saudi Arabia under attack could dictate the timing of a war against Iran  HaaretzView / Saudi Arabia faces its toughest moment of war  Semafor
articles.full_text:
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman wanted to make his kingdom a magnet for investment, tourism and the world’s biggest sporting events. Now drones and missiles launched from Yemen are slamming into Saudi cities, drawing the kingdom deeper into the regional turmoil he hoped to leave behind.
The civil war in Yemen erupted once again this summer and significantly intensified last month, breaking years of relative calm. Saudi Arabia has for 11 years tried to contain the conflict on its southern border through military force and diplomacy – first waging war with the Iran-allied Houthi group, then pursuing peace talks with them and restoring diplomatic talks with their backer, Iran.
Despite the efforts, a series of miscalculations has left Riyadh exposed to further conflict in Yemen, experts say. Saudi Arabia’s ended its longstanding partnership with the UAE late last year over its backing of a rival force in Yemen, misjudged President Donald Trump’s willingness to back it if it needed support, and struggled to organize disintegrated armed factions fighting the Houthis in Yemen.
Now, Riyadh is trying to regain its footing by supporting its Yemeni partners in yet another campaign against the Houthis, an operation named “Yemen’s Dawn.”
Prince Mohammed’s ambitions to transform his kingdom have already faced several challenges since his rise to power more than a decade ago. Today, they’re coming under further strain as multi-front attacks on oil infrastructure cut into exports, major projects are canceled, and the kingdom is pulled into a war with no clear way out.
At least three people, including a Saudi pilot, were killed this week after Houthi forces struck several airports in the kingdom, according to Saudi Arabia. Regional turmoil has forced the suspension of star-studded film festivals, award shows, and music concerts this year. Meanwhile, the kingdom’s flagship financial conference, which is expected to draw high-profile business leaders at the end of October, is coming under pressure amid the strikes.
“They just needed the conflict to stay (as) far away from them as possible without the Houthis disrupting their transformation plans,” Michael Ratney, the former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia, told CNN. “Now they find themselves in the middle of it.”
A hasty UAE exit
When Saudi warplanes struck a shipment of military vehicles sent to Yemen by the UAE last year, a decade-old alliance between two nations fighting Iran’s influence in Yemen shattered, leaving the kingdom to contend with the crisis alone after Abu Dhabi withdrew its forces. The break with the UAE shocked the region. Saudi Arabia launched a rare media campaign against its neighbor, accusing it of fueling instability in Sudan and Yemen. Saudi commentators publicly cast the UAE as a younger sibling rebelling against a wiser one.
Saudi Arabia is the “head and body” on which regional stability rests, wrote prominent Saudi journalist Dawood Al-Shirian in January. “If (Saudi Arabia) stumbles, the entire system is disrupted and the Gulf scatters.”
As Riyadh pressed for dominance in the Gulf, the ground shifted in Yemen. The four-year ceasefire with the Houthis was already fragile, and the rapid UAE withdrawal as demanded by Riyadh left thousands of fighters who had spent a decade under Abu Dhabi’s command disoriented by Riyadh’s strategy.
Fighters allied with the UAE say Abu Dhabi’s departure left a power vacuum the Saudis didn’t fill.
“There wasn’t a proper transition when the Emiratis left,” a southern Yemeni official, who asked to remain anonymous to speak freely to CNN, said. “It was frightening how different things became. The Emiratis’ command and control was very efficient, and the Saudis did not replace this efficiency.”
CNN reached out to the Saudi government for comment on whether the forces fighting the Houthis on the ground received enough support and whether there was a proper transition.
Lack of preparation
Eight weeks after the UAE withdrawal, the US and Israel launched a war on Iran, killing supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The moves sparked a conflict that has plunged the region into unprecedented turmoil and placed Washington’s allies, including Saudi Arabia, in Iran’s crosshairs.
The timing was unfortunate for Saudi Arabia, several experts say. After contending with the UAE-backed separatist push in Yemen, the US and Israel triggered a regional war. And despite years of trying to stop the war from breaking out in Yemen, the pressure Trump imposed on Iran was expected to eventually trigger a Houthi push on the kingdom.
“The Saudis had to respond after being attacked by an enemy force on their territory… so there was always going to be a response,” Ratney, the former US ambassador, said.
Even as Iranian missiles struck the kingdom from the east, Saudi attention focused on the south. The Houthis, still formally in a truce with Riyadh, appeared unwilling to aid their Iranian partners. Tehran instead drew the Saudis in.
In July, Iran sent a commercial plane to carry a Houthi delegation to Khamenei’s funeral in Tehran, defying a Saudi air blockade of Yemen. Riyadh struck the Houthi-held airport in Sanaa to prevent the plane from landing. The rebel group retaliated by declaring the truce dead and announced a naval blockade on Saudi ships. It also started a lightning offensive down Yemen’s coast, seizing strategic territory at the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in the largest escalation since 2022.
The Houthis attacked Saudi oil facilities and pipelines, disrupting crude supplies and sending prices sharply higher. Saudi forces answered with hundreds of airstrikes.
“The Saudis have made several mistakes and failures,” Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen with the International Crisis Group think tank, told CNN, noting that Riyadh hadn’t prepared for a Houthi offensive and lacked coordination with allied Yemeni forces it inherited from the UAE.
“The areas they’ve lost created morale issues with their allies and now it’s a big challenge for the Saudis as the Houthis have more advanced weaponry which managed to reach several cities in Saudi Arabia,” he said.
‘Unpredictable’ Trump
Another miscalculation by Saudi Arabia was its reliance on continued American support, experts say. Despite signing a new defense pact with Washington last year and being designated a Major Non-NATO Ally by the US, Riyadh has been disappointed by what it sees as waning US commitment to its security.
Prince Mohammed spoke twice with Trump last month, urging him to strike the Houthis, sources told CNN at the time, but Trump declined to intervene. Washington instead met the Houthis in Oman, seeking to protect its own ceasefire with the group, which made it clear that its war was with Saudi Arabia alone, thus allowing US vessels to traverse the Red Sea freely.
For a military that has built its “entire worldview” around partnering with the US, the Saudis are realizing how unpredictable Trump is, said Ratney.
“It was never their concept or the structure of their military to fight these wars by themselves,” he said. “Under a normal US presidency, if something like this happens, we would’ve helped our partner in what would’ve been a rational and considered process.
“Now we don’t have that process, and it ultimately comes down to: what does Trump think? And the Saudis probably feel exposed as a result,” he added.
Saudi Arabia has since looked elsewhere. Last month, Prince Mohammed flew to Egypt to meet President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, then invited UAE Vice President Sheik Mansour bin Zayed to Riyadh a few weeks later to discuss regional developments. France agreed to deploy defense assets, including military personnel. Britain said it would send an aircraft to help refuel Saudi jets. More than 100 American military advisers are on the ground providing intelligence and targeting support under a newly established joint forces command.
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agreed on Monday to “activate collective deterrence measures” under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement after an emergency meeting in Riyadh. The pact, set up earlier this year, is meant to coordinate defense and security cooperation among the three. Forces loyal to the UAE also appear to be taking part in the offensive, a sign of at least a partial thaw between the kingdom and the UAE.
A regional solution
But experts warn that outside support and early gains by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government will not settle the conflict. Infighting remains common among the factions, and there is still no clear political end state.
A sustained push against Iranian-backed forces, analysts say, would require organization, regional backing, funding, and logistics that the current coalition has not yet shown it can sustain.
“They need to unify their command centers, they need to resolve the issues they have between the various factions within the group,” Hisham Al Omeisy, a senior Yemen adviser for the European Institute of Peace told CNN’s Becky Anderson. “Territorial gains they’ve made would mean nothing if the (Saudi-backed) Yemeni government cannot maintain control over those areas.”
Many experts said however that the fighting in Yemen is connected to the US war in Iran, and as long as the conflict between Washington and Tehran is ongoing, the Iranians will continue having a powerful incentive to watch the Houthis disrupt Saudi Arabia.
Gulf states could manage to secure a separate diplomatic solution with Iran, analysts say, or escalate their military strikes to eliminate Houthi leadership.
“Neither of those scenarios fix the conflict in Yemen in any near term,” Ratney said. “The Saudis will have to just figure out an imperfect path ahead.”

articles.title: 12 killed and over 300 hurt in latest attack on Riyadh airport, Saudi authorities say - AP News
articles.summary: 12 killed and over 300 hurt in latest attack on Riyadh airport, Saudi authorities say  AP NewsSaudi Arabia’s Riyadh Airport Attacked Again, After Days of Houthi Strikes  The New York TimesAt least 12 killed and hundreds injured in attack on Riyadh airport  YahooIran war live: 12 killed in Riyadh, Trump to speak with Saudi Arabia’s MBS  Al JazeeraHouthis Bombard Saudi Air Links in Effort to Cut Kingdom Off From Rest of World  WSJ
articles.full_text:
CAIRO (AP) — The latest attack on the international airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital of Riyadh killed 12 people and injured over 300 others, civil aviation authorities said early Sunday, with some in critical condition. A Saudi-led coalition blamed Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen.
It was the deadliest attack in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war, whose fronts have expanded to include the recent surge in fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces.
A missile struck a King Khalid International Airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak to the media.
The Saudi statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said the injured were being treated at several hospitals.
Footage posted on social media following the attack and analyzed by The Associated Press shows emergency vehicles outside the airport.
Trump said he would consider joining strikes against rebels
The attack — the latest of several in the past week on the airport — is expected to increase Saudi pressure on allies including the United States to provide military support for the kingdom, which has seemingly tried to avoid all-out war with the Houthis.
Shortly after the attack on Saturday afternoon, U.S. President Donald Trump said he was evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the rebels. “We may. We’re going to look at it,” he said. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”
Trump later Saturday said he planned to speak to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and said “what happened in Saudi Arabia is not acceptable.” Asked if the U.S. might get involved, Trump responded, “We’ll find out.”
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged in a social media post that an American citizen had been killed in the attack, which he condemned.
“These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now,” he said.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed them for the attack, calling it a “fully-fledged war crime” and vowing a firm response. The airport has no military facilities.
There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.
The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot. The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis.
Saudi civil aviation authorities earlier Saturday said airport operations were suspended. The airport had a heavy police presence, with all entrances blocked, and lights around the complex were dimmed. Flights diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport.
Also Saturday, U.S. Central Command said a fighter jet struck and disabled a commercial cargo vessel with a precision munition in the Gulf of Oman, part of U.S. efforts to maintain a naval blockade of Iranian ports. The Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica had departed an Iranian port and did not heed repeated warnings. The ship’s crew was unharmed, CENTCOM said.
For Iran, the fighting puts pressure on a key US ally
The attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world’s top oil exporter, have rattled markets and the region. And yet the Saudi energy ministry hours after the latest one was still promoting a major international energy conference set to begin in Riyadh on Sunday.
Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the sidelines of the Iran war. Now the rebels are a way for Tehran to apply pressure on a key U.S. ally.
The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015 when the kingdom entered Yemen’s civil war on behalf of the internationally recognized government. Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land. That revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas.
Now fighting has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea. Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.
While the Houthis have said they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for the one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist. The Houthis previously attacked dozens of ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A U.S. bombing campaign sharply limited that.
Saudi Arabia has run low on interceptors, officials say
Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told the AP last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.
Officials have said U.S. assistance has included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the latest offensive against the Houthis.
On Saturday, Saudi Arabia said its foreign minister and Omani counterpart spoke by phone about the importance of “supporting diplomatic solutions to de-escalate tensions” in the region. Oman, which lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, has played a mediator role at times in the region.
Saudi flight disruptions are growing
The Houthis this week warned global airlines “for the last time” about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations.
Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines were among airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency had expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, noting the Houthis’ ability to strike targets deeper inside the kingdom, including Riyadh, and a “greater focus on aviation infrastructure.”
The missile and drone attacks and interception efforts “create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft,” it said.
Two regional officials said Houthi attacks on the Riyadh airport on Thursday damaged three planes. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to brief the media. The Saudi national carrier said one of its aircraft was damaged while it was on the ground, with no passengers on board.
Meanwhile, Saudi authorities warned the public this week that “filming, publishing or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability.”
___
Anna reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Collin Binkley in Washington and Sally Abou AlJoud in Beirut contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump takes Clinton lawsuit to Supreme Court after $1M sanctions
articles.summary: President Donald Trump asked the U.S. Supreme Court on Friday to revive his dismissed lawsuit accusing his 2016 Democratic rival Hillary Clinton, former FBI Director James Comey an...
articles.full_text:
President Donald Trump asked the U.S. Supreme Court on Friday to revive his dismissed lawsuit accusing his 2016 Democratic rival Hillary Clinton, former FBI Director James Comey and others of conspiring to undermine his campaign by linking it to Russia.
Trump filed the appeal after a federal judge dismissed the lawsuit and ordered him and one of his lawyers to pay nearly $1 million in sanctions for bringing what the court described as a “frivolous” case. A federal appeals court later upheld both the dismissal and the sanctions.
Trump filed the lawsuit in 2022, after leaving office following his 2020 election defeat. The lengthy complaint, filed in federal court in Florida, named Clinton, Comey, former British intelligence officer Christopher Steele, the Democratic National Committee and numerous other defendants.
Trump, who has repeatedly pursued legal action against political opponents, alleged that Clinton and her allies conspired before the 2016 election to discredit him by promoting what he called a “false narrative” that his campaign had colluded with Russia.
The lawsuit included claims of racketeering and conspiracy to commit injurious falsehood, among other allegations.
Trump defeated Clinton in the 2016 election despite losing the national popular vote. He served his first term as president from 2017 to 2021.
U.S. government officials have accused Russia of interfering in the 2016 election. An investigation led by former FBI Director Robert Mueller documented extensive contacts between the Trump campaign and Russian operatives who sought to influence the election in Trump's favor. Trump has dismissed allegations of Russian interference as a “hoax.”
Since losing to Democrat Joe Biden in 2020, Trump has repeatedly made false claims of widespread voting fraud in that election. He regained the presidency by defeating Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024 and has continued to make those claims.
U.S. District Judge Donald Middlebrooks dismissed Trump's lawsuit against Clinton, citing numerous deficiencies, including that Trump had waited too long to bring some of his claims. The judge likened the lawsuit to a “two-hundred-page political manifesto outlining his grievances against those that have opposed him.”
Middlebrooks later ordered Trump and his lead attorney in the case, Alina Habba, to pay nearly $1 million in fees and costs. He imposed the sanctions for bringing a lawsuit that he said was intended “to dishonestly advance a political narrative.” The judge also criticized Trump and his lawyers for a “continuing pattern of misuse of the courts.”
Middlebrooks found that the lawsuit relied on abusive litigation tactics, contained “knowingly false” factual allegations and advanced “frivolous” legal theories.
The Atlanta-based 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the judge's rulings in 2025, including the sanctions.
“Many of Trump's and Habba's legal arguments were indeed frivolous,” the 11th Circuit said.
In court filings, lawyers for Trump and Habba argued that the lower courts' decisions were having a “profound impact on the presidency, and the nation as a whole.”
Mueller, who was appointed special counsel by the Justice Department, issued a report in 2019 detailing his investigation. The report concluded that Russia “interfered in the 2016 presidential election in sweeping and systematic fashion,” but said the investigation “did not establish that members of the Trump campaign conspired or coordinated with the Russian government in its election interference activities.”
Mueller also reported finding “numerous links” between the Trump campaign and Russia, adding that the campaign “expected it would benefit” from Moscow's efforts to influence the election in Trump's favor.
Trump's then-Attorney General William Barr appointed another special counsel, John Durham, in 2019 to investigate potential misconduct by the FBI.
In a 2023 report, Durham concluded that the FBI lacked “actual evidence” to investigate Trump's 2016 presidential campaign and relied too heavily on information supplied by Trump's political opponents to launch the probe.
Last year, Trump's Justice Department indicted Comey, one of several of the president's adversaries to face criminal charges, accusing him of making false statements and obstructing Congress after allegations that he had lied about authorizing leaks to the news media. A federal judge subsequently dismissed the indictment, finding that the prosecutor Trump had selected to pursue the case was unlawfully appointed.
Steele, working for an opposition research firm hired by a law firm on behalf of the Clinton campaign and the Democratic National Committee, produced a dossier alleging ties between Trump's campaign and Russia, along with other salacious claims that Trump denied.

articles.title: Israeli forces shoot AA photojournalist during West Bank harvest
articles.summary: Israeli forces shot and wounded Anadolu Agency (AA) Palestinian photojournalist Issam Rimawi with a rubber-coated bullet Saturday as he covered the olive harvest and confrontations...
articles.full_text:
Israeli forces shot and wounded Anadolu Agency (AA) Palestinian photojournalist Issam Rimawi with a rubber-coated bullet Saturday as he covered the olive harvest and confrontations between Palestinian farmers and Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
The incident occurred in Deir Nizam, near Ramallah, where farmers had appealed to activists for help harvesting their olives after attacks by Israeli settlers prevented them from reaching their land.
Following the appeal, farmers and a large group of activists headed to the olive groves to gather the crops. Israeli settlers subsequently arrived and attacked the Palestinians and activists, according to local reports.
Israeli soldiers later reached the scene and fired tear gas and rubber-coated bullets at the Palestinians, siding with the settlers, according to Palestinian accounts.
Rimawi, who was documenting the harvest and ensuing confrontations, was struck in his right calf by a rubber-coated bullet fired by Israeli soldiers. He was taken to a nearby hospital for treatment.
Speaking after the shooting, Rimawi said a scuffle had broken out between Israeli settlers and Palestinians before Israeli forces arrived and intervened.
He said soldiers opened fire on the Palestinians despite journalists wearing clearly identifiable press vests and helmets.
The shooting occurred during the annual olive harvest, a vital source of income for Palestinian farming communities and an important part of their cultural heritage.
The season frequently brings heightened tensions as farmers face attacks, restrictions on access to their land and damage to their crops and trees.
Palestinian monitoring bodies have documented numerous attacks on farmers and agricultural property during the early stages of the 2026 harvest season.
Reported incidents include the destruction of olive trees, fires and intimidation aimed at preventing Palestinians from reaching their groves.
Damage to agricultural land has added to the pressures facing Palestinian farmers, many of whom depend on olive production for their livelihoods. Restrictions on access to farmland and settlement-related activities have further complicated harvesting efforts.
Rimawi, an experienced photojournalist who has covered events across the occupied West Bank for years, has previously been injured while reporting on protests and confrontations involving Israeli forces and settlers.
His latest injury highlights the dangers facing journalists covering violence and restrictions on Palestinian communities, particularly during the olive harvest.
Since October 2023, Israeli military operations and settler attacks have intensified across the occupied West Bank, resulting in rising casualties, widespread arrests and damage to Palestinian homes, farmland and other property.
Palestinian figures cited in reports put the number of Palestinians killed during that period at 1,210, with 13,350 injured and approximately 26,000 arrested.
The figures cover violence involving Israeli forces and settlers and reflect the broader escalation across the territory.

articles.title: Indonesia’s raging wildfires endanger orangutans, scorch forests
articles.summary: Wildfires raging across parts of Indonesia’s Borneo island are threatening endangered orangutans, forcing rescuers to evacuate animals found injured, stranded or struggling to surv...
articles.full_text:
Wildfires raging across parts of Indonesia’s Borneo island are threatening endangered orangutans, forcing rescuers to evacuate animals found injured, stranded or struggling to survive amid thick smoke and scorched forests.
Among dozens of orangutans rescued from fires across Sumatra and Borneo in recent months was a female Bornean orangutan known as Novita.
Rescuers found her clinging to a nearly leafless tree as dense smoke engulfed the charred landscape of the Katune forest in Central Kalimantan province, said Jamartin Sihite, chairman of the Borneo Orangutan Survival Foundation.
“The palms of her hands and the soles of her feet suffered burns that were likely sustained when Novita crossed a burned area while trying to reach a tree,” Sihite told The Associated Press in an interview. He said Novita, estimated to be 3 to 4 years old, was tranquilized, given oxygen and intravenous fluids, and taken to the rehabilitation center in Nyaru Menteng.
Once her burns have healed, Novita will be evaluated to determine whether she can climb and survive in her natural environment, Sihite said.
“We have previously released orangutans missing several fingers, and they were still able to survive in the forest, so we remain hopeful that Novita can eventually return to the wild.”
Forest and land fires in Indonesia have worsened this year as El Niño intensifies a prolonged dry season, affecting not only the Indonesian part of Borneo but also some regions of Sumatra. Water shortages in affected areas have hampered firefighting efforts, while Japan has provided firefighting assistance on the island.
A male orangutan named Sampurna, believed to be around 20 years old, was found struggling to breathe by residents early last month on a palm oil plantation in West Kalimantan’s Ketapang district, an area affected by wildfires. He died hours after being rescued, Indonesia’s Forestry Ministry said.
More than 270 wild animals in Kalimantan had been rescued, rehabilitated or guided to safer habitats as of Saturday, the ministry said.
Government data showed that more than 202,000 hectares (499,000 acres) of land burned between January and July. The independent Nusantara Atlas project, which monitors fires using satellite imagery, estimated that nearly 896,000 hectares (2.2 million acres) had burned by the end of August.
Toxic haze and smoke have also caused a health crisis in neighboring countries. The smoke has drifted as far as the Philippines, more than 800 kilometers (500 miles) away. In Malaysia, authorities declared an emergency last week in Sarawak, on the Malaysian part of Borneo.
Novita’s case highlights the impact of forest and peatland fires on wildlife as well as people, said Andi Muhammad Kadhafi, head of the Central Kalimantan Natural Resources Conservation Agency, a government body.
“Wildfires do not only affect humans but can also threaten wildlife and their habitats,” he said. “Fire prevention, habitat protection, monitoring and rapid response need to go hand in hand.”

articles.title: Amelia Earhart mystery draws new search to remote Pacific island
articles.summary: A team of U.S.-based marine archaeologists has set sail for a remote island in the western Pacific in hopes of uncovering new evidence in one of the 20th century’s most enduring my...
articles.full_text:
A team of U.S.-based marine archaeologists has set sail for a remote island in the western Pacific in hopes of uncovering new evidence in one of the 20th century’s most enduring mysteries: the 1937 disappearance of famed aviator Amelia Earhart.
Supported by Purdue University, which has long been associated with Earhart and her legacy, the team aims to determine whether an object detected beneath the waters of the island’s lagoon in satellite imagery six years ago is the wreckage of her twin-engine Lockheed Electra 10-E aircraft.
If confirmed, the discovery would lend decisive support to a longstanding theory that Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, crash-landed on or near the coral-ringed atoll and died as castaways, hundreds of miles from their intended refueling stop.
The expedition departed Los Angeles earlier this month and was expected to reach Nikumaroro on Tuesday, Oct. 13, local time. The uninhabited island lies in the remote Phoenix Islands, part of the Pacific nation of Kiribati.
“Finding Amelia Earhart’s Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime,” Richard Pettigrew, head of the Archaeological Legacy Institute in Eugene, Oregon, who is leading the effort in conjunction with Purdue, said in press materials for the mission.
Purdue general counsel and expedition member Steve Schultz, who was in Fiji conducting advance work for the expedition last week, said in an interview: “This would be solving one of the great mysteries in aviation history, certainly one of the great mysteries of the 20th century.”
The mission has its skeptics. Chief among them is rival Earhart explorer Ric Gillespie, co-founder of TIGHAR, short for The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery, and author of the 2024 book “One More Good Flight: The Amelia Earhart Tragedy.”
Gillespie has led a dozen expeditions of his own to the atoll over three decades and is the leading proponent of the Nikumaroro castaway theory. But he predicted the Pettigrew-Purdue team would find no airplane wreckage or anything else of consequence left on the island.
The Purdue team credits Gillespie with laying the foundation for the theory it hopes to prove. It also cites a compelling body of evidence he has amassed over the years, including human artifacts recovered on the island, such as a 1930s-era glass cosmetic jar for freckle cream and remnants of a jackknife like one Earhart carried on the plane.
Gillespie’s investigation also encompassed modern forensic analysis of records documenting measurements of skeletal remains found on the island in the 1940s; logs of radio transmission bearings from distress calls picked up by wireless operators in the days immediately after Earhart vanished; and a photograph taken of the island’s shoreline months later showing an object that Gillespie said appears to be the Electra’s landing gear.
In a Reuters interview last week, Gillespie said he believes the plane has since been lost to history, eventually swept by tides off the coral flat where it had landed largely intact and carried into the sea, where it sank and broke apart in the surf.
Two previous attempts to locate the plane’s wreckage in the surrounding ocean, including a 2019 operation conducted by marine archaeologist Robert Ballard, known for discovering the wreck of the Titanic, proved fruitless, Gillespie said.
A plane-shaped sonar image from elsewhere on the seafloor turned out to be a pile of rocks.
“I’d love to find that airplane. It ain’t gonna happen,” Gillespie said.
Pettigrew and his team are betting otherwise. To them, the multibranched shape first noticed in a 2020 satellite image resembles an aircraft fuselage and wings. They assert that the object, or part of it, has since been spotted in earlier aerial images of the island’s lagoon dating to 1938.
Gillespie said he is certain the object in question was actually a fallen pandanus tree, a palm-like evergreen native to the region, that washed into the lagoon.
“You can see the root ball. You can see the branches,” Gillespie said in the interview. “It’s a tree. People see what they want to see.”
The official U.S. government view has long been that the Electra ran out of fuel and crashed at sea near its intended destination, Howland Island, another small island about 400 miles northwest of Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.
Earhart was last seen taking off in her Electra on July 2, 1937, from Papua New Guinea, en route to Gardner, about 2,500 miles (4,000 kilometers) to the east, during a multistage attempt to become the first woman to pilot a plane around the world.
Definitive radio contact with the plane was lost the next day after Earhart, 39, reported that “gas is running low,” followed by her final known transmission giving her geographical line of position.
The disappearance prompted the largest U.S. government search ever undertaken for a missing aircraft, including a flyover of Gardner, but no trace of the Electra or its crew was found at the time.
The $900,000 Purdue mission, consisting of 17 people, plans to remain on Nikumaroro for five days before making the six-day return boat trip to the Kiribati capital, Tarawa, according to Schultz.
Purdue, based in West Lafayette, Indiana, would ultimately seek to bring back any pieces of the Lockheed Electra that might be recovered.
Earhart was essentially a visiting faculty member at Purdue for two years, serving as a women’s career counselor and adviser to the school’s aeronautics department. A Purdue research grant paid for development of the Electra, which she called her “flying laboratory.”
Purdue lawyer Schultz said that if the plane were found, no artifacts would be removed from it on this trip. Any effort to extract the aircraft wreckage would require further permission from the Kiribati government, he said.

articles.title: Russian strikes kill 8 in Ukraine as Trump’s diesel deal backfires
articles.summary: Russian strikes killed at least eight people, including three children, in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region on Saturday, as President Donald Trump’s announcement of a deal to import R...
articles.full_text:
Russian strikes killed at least eight people, including three children, in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region on Saturday, as President Donald Trump’s announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel drew sharp criticism from Kyiv over concerns that the shipments would help finance Moscow’s war.
At least 16 people were wounded when Russian aerial bombs struck residential buildings in the southeastern region, Ivan Fedorov, co-chair of the regional defense council, said.
The attack came amid an intensifying Russian bombardment that has killed more than 55 people across Ukraine over the past four days, according to Ukrainian officials.
The two countries remain largely deadlocked along the front line more than 4.5 years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion, while their forces continue to wage a long-range aerial war.
The latest casualties underscored the mounting pressure on Ukraine as it struggles to defend its territory against increasingly deadly Russian attacks.
They also came a day after Trump announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply diesel to the United States and global markets, marking a significant shift in Washington’s approach to Moscow as fuel prices rise ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the deal, warning that allowing Russia to expand its petroleum exports would provide Moscow with additional revenue to sustain its military campaign.
“Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in the war, which must be ended, not prolonged,” Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram on Friday.
He warned that Moscow would repay the agreement with further attacks and what he described as “terror and perfidy,” arguing that the arrangement would encourage Russia to continue its offensive while undermining Washington’s efforts to end the conflict.
In a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington, Zelenskyy described the agreement as “a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners.”
The Ukrainian leader was particularly angered that Trump announced the deal while his special envoy, Steve Witkoff, and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian officials in Miami to discuss a proposal to end the war. Zelenskyy said the proposed fuel arrangement had not been raised during those talks.
“I believe our team is simply being used as a smoke screen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” he said.
In an interview with the U.S. news outlet Axios, Zelenskyy also described the agreement as “not fair and not honest,” warning that any relaxation of restrictions on Russian energy exports would weaken pressure on the Kremlin.
Trump defended the deal, saying the United States needed additional supplies to help ease prices.
“We need oil for the world, and this is diesel, which is what we need, so we're very happy to get it,” he said.
Trump announced the agreement on his Truth Social platform Friday after a phone call with Putin that had been expected to focus on a suspected case of plague in Russia.
Instead, Trump said the Russian leader had agreed to arrange substantial diesel shipments, beginning with more than 300,000 metric tons immediately, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons shortly afterward. A further 3 million tons could arrive within a relatively short period, he said, depending on supply conditions.
The Kremlin confirmed that Russia was prepared to supply oil and petroleum products to international markets.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak separately announced the immediate lifting of Moscow’s ban on diesel exports, according to the state news agency TASS. Novak outlined a schedule of 300,000 tons in October, 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons in December, contingent on repairs to refineries damaged by Ukrainian drone attacks.
Russia produced about 7 million tons of diesel per month last year, but its production capacity has since fallen by roughly half, according to the figures cited in reports on the agreement.
The initial 300,000-ton shipment would represent only a small share of global diesel demand and is unlikely to significantly reduce prices on its own. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, that volume would theoretically cover just over 14 hours of U.S. consumption of diesel and other distillate fuels.
The agreement nevertheless represents a notable reversal in Washington’s approach to Russia. Last month, Trump signed legislation granting his administration broad powers to impose additional sanctions on Moscow, including measures targeting the energy exports that help fund its war against Ukraine.
Following the announcement, the U.S. Treasury Department issued a temporary exemption from sanctions allowing the sale, supply, unloading and import of Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
The move comes as the Trump administration faces competing pressures to contain fuel costs at home while maintaining leverage over Russia. Rising energy prices have become a growing political concern ahead of the November midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress.
Fuel costs have surged worldwide amid the U.S. war with Iran and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical passage for global oil supplies. Some Republicans have also blamed the conflict with Iran for the rise in prices.
Trump has repeatedly criticized Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries, arguing that they contribute to fuel shortages and higher costs. He has urged Kyiv to halt the strikes, which target infrastructure that helps sustain Russia’s energy exports and war effort.
In his latest social media post, Trump said the diesel agreement, combined with what he described as Washington’s “TOTAL CONTROL” of the Strait of Hormuz, would drive prices sharply lower.
“Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,” he wrote.
Despite his criticism of the diesel agreement, Zelenskyy reiterated Ukraine’s willingness to stop attacking Russian refineries if Moscow agreed to end its strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
“We are proposing precisely such an agreement to America and believe that the strength of the United States is sufficient to achieve such a compromise,” he wrote.
The proposal reflects Kyiv’s push for reciprocal restrictions on attacks against energy facilities, which have become central targets in the war.
Russian strikes have repeatedly damaged Ukraine’s infrastructure, while Ukrainian forces have targeted Russian refineries in an effort to disrupt fuel production and the revenues supporting Moscow’s military campaign.
Zelenskyy warned that easing sanctions or allowing Russia to expand its energy sales would signal weakness and encourage the Kremlin to take Washington less seriously.

articles.title: India detains ‘Cockroach’ leaders amid voter list protests
articles.summary: Indian authorities mounted a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi on Saturday, detaining thousands of protesters as the country’s youth-led “Cockroach” movement sought to e...
articles.full_text:
Indian authorities mounted a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi on Saturday, detaining thousands of protesters as the country’s youth-led “Cockroach” movement sought to escalate a nationwide campaign against a contentious revision of voter lists.
The dispute has fueled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.
Police intercepted demonstrators before they could reach Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the heart of the capital.
Officers chased away some protesters and detained many others, with several dragged away and bundled into police vehicles before being taken to temporary detention centers.
Several leaders of the “Cockroach” movement were also detained before reaching the venue, severely disrupting the planned demonstration before it could begin.
The security operation extended well beyond the protest site, with police setting up checkpoints on roads leading into the capital.
Officers stopped buses, cars and other vehicles and searched them for demonstrators as authorities moved to prevent protesters from gathering in the city.
Jantar Mantar was barricaded, while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear gas launchers were stationed along key routes. Restrictions on mobile internet access and movement in parts of the city added to the hurdles facing protesters.
Police said Friday they had denied permission for the protest because the request was submitted late.
The scale of the crackdown underscored the authorities’ determination to disrupt a fast-growing protest campaign that has mobilized thousands of young people, drawn opposition support and intensified scrutiny of Modi.
The protests also come at a politically sensitive time, months after demonstrations led by the “Cockroach” movement over exam paper leaks forced Modi’s education minister to resign in July.
Movement leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were expected to be at the forefront of Saturday’s protest, were detained after arriving at Delhi airport from Mumbai.
A video shared by the “Cockroach Janta Party” on X showed police boarding the aircraft and detaining the three men.
“The preplanned interception by Delhi police aims to cripple the leadership of today’s peaceful demonstrations before they even reach the protest site,” the movement said in a statement.
Loudspeakers around the protest site warned that gatherings of five or more people were banned in parts of New Delhi as authorities imposed sweeping security restrictions rarely seen in the capital. Journalists also faced restrictions in some areas.
Some protesters nevertheless broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and election authorities before being detained.
“We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force. Shouldn’t we fight for our rights?” said Tanya Negi, a college student who traveled from Mumbai with two friends and arrived early Saturday. “Why is Modi afraid of India’s young people?”
The crackdown drew criticism from opposition leaders, who accused the government of curbing dissent.
“Is there a democracy in this country? A total siege over the city. Citizens are being driven out,” opposition lawmaker John Brittas told The Associated Press.
The protests center on the Election Commission of India’s Special Intensive Revision, which the opposition says has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters.
Protesters are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the revision, which has removed more than 130 million names from voter lists so far.
The Election Commission and the government reject allegations of voter manipulation, saying the revision is intended to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries.
The dispute has become a rallying point for opposition parties seeking to challenge Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.
Saturday’s planned demonstration followed days of protests in the capital, where opposition lawmakers also stepped up their campaign. Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi was briefly detained by police.
Gandhi and other opposition leaders have accused the commission of conducting the voter revision in a way that benefits Modi’s party. The opposition says voters more likely to support its parties have been disproportionately affected by the removals, while BJP supporters have been spared or added to the lists.
The commission and the government deny the allegations.
For the “Cockroach” movement, the voter list dispute offers an opportunity to broaden its campaign.
The movement began online in May and gained prominence through demonstrations, sit-ins and hunger strikes over alleged exam paper leaks. Those protests culminated in the resignation of Modi’s education minister in July, a rare political setback for a prime minister who has maintained a firm hold on national power for more than 12 years.
For Modi, the protests pose a challenge midway through his third term, though their political impact remains unclear. National elections are not due until 2029, but state elections next year in BJP-ruled Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous state, and Gujarat, Modi’s home state, will test the party’s standing.
